Précis

A claim-bounded complete reasoning record for Erdős #251. It retains the prime-gap summation identities, rationality-to-shift reductions, small-mismatch consumers, coefficient countermodels, finite evidence, and all registered families. No theorem produces the required cofinal mismatch for the actual prime-gap series, so irrationality remains open.

This paper owns the complete problem-specific reasoning surface for Erdős #251, including all registered result families and their boundaries.

It is not authority for the validity of claims tagged Lean, which belongs to the cited kernel-checked source, or a solution to Erdős #251, which remains open.

Introduction

Throughout, the primes are indexed from zero: 𝑝0 =2p0=2, 𝑝1 =3p1=3, 𝑝2 =5p2=5, and 𝑔𝑛 =𝑝𝑛+1 −𝑝𝑛gn=pn+1−pn. Erdős Problem #251 concerns

Π=∑𝑛≥0𝑝𝑛2𝑛+1=2/2+3/4+5/8+7/16+⋯,Π=∑n≥0pn2n+1=2/2+3/4+5/8+7/16+⋯,

with the question recorded in [1], and . The supplied catalogue snapshot records no unconditional solution [22]; no refreshed status of the live catalogue is assumed in this revision. The first values are

𝑖0123456789𝑝𝑖2357111317192329𝑔𝑖1224242462i0123456789pi2357111317192329gi1224242462

so 𝑔0 =1g0=1 and every later gap is even, the primes after 22 being odd. A second normalisation with denominator 2𝑖2i also occurs, and at every finite horizon it is exactly twice this one,

𝑛−1∑𝑖=0𝑝𝑖2𝑖=2𝑛−1∑𝑖=0𝑝𝑖2𝑖+1,∑i=0n−1pi2i=2∑i=0n−1pi2i+1,

the factor-of-two normalisation. A factor of two does not change rationality, so no result below depends on the choice; the identity is stated so that the indexing cannot drift silently.

Notation.

ℕ ={0,1,2,…}N={0,1,2,…} and ℕ>0 ={1,2,…}N>0={1,2,…}. We write 𝜑φ for Euler’s totient function, den⁡𝑞den⁡q for the denominator of a rational number 𝑞q written in lowest terms, dist⁡(𝑥,ℤ)dist⁡(x,Z) for the distance from a real number 𝑥x to the nearest integer, and Irr⁡(𝑥)Irr⁡(x) for the assertion that 𝑥x is irrational. A rational number is called integral when it is the image of an integer. A sequence (𝑎𝑛)(an) is eventually periodic with period ℎ ≥1h≥1 when 𝑎𝑛+ℎ =𝑎𝑛an+h=an for every sufficiently large 𝑛n. A set 𝐴 ⊆ℕA⊆N has density zero when |𝐴 ∩[1,𝑥]| =𝑜(𝑥)|A∩[1,x]|=o(x), and a property holds for almost all indices when its exceptional set has density zero. A sum over an empty range of indices is zero.

Sparse congruence-preserving perturbations

The sparse construction preserves cumulative residues as well as coefficient residues. Two adjacent corrections provide a free weighted digit while fixing their unweighted total. A third coordinate is needed to repair the cumulative residue before that pair. We account separately for its location, size and contribution to the series.

The pair identities, modular repair and conditional interval filling have formal counterparts in . The supplied index marks the arbitrary-word interval theorem, its rational-target consequence, the polylogarithmic interval theorem, the block total-variation bound and the uniform bounded-test theorem as ci_checked. The full existential conclusions are therefore covered by the supplied verification record. The formal construction is a one-site residue-feedback construction, not the buffered-triple schedule printed above. Agreement of theorem statements must not be confused with identity of these witnesses. There is no Comparator entry for this theorem. Applied to prime gaps, the construction makes no assertion that the corrected cumulative positions remain prime.

Corollary 2.2 (arbitrarily local target intervals). For the arbitrary-word sparse theorem, the target interval can additionally be required to lie in (𝐴,𝐴 +𝜂)(A,A+η) for any prescribed 𝜂 >0η>0.

Proof. In the general schedule, every supported entry satisfies 𝑒𝑛 ≤𝑛en≤n. Start beyond an integer 𝐾′K′ with ∑𝑛≥𝐾′𝑛2−(𝑛+1) =(𝐾′ +1)2−𝐾′ <𝜂∑n≥K′n2−(n+1)=(K′+1)2−K′<η. The complete interval of corrections has positive lower endpoint and upper endpoint at most this sum. This strengthens the location of the interval, not a claim that every number above 𝐴A is attainable under one fixed envelope. ◻

Context and mathematical dependencies

Relation to prior work.

The passage from the primes to their gaps is already public. Tao posted on the problem’s forum thread on 7 October 2025 that summation by parts makes the question equivalent to irrationality of ∑𝑛(𝑝𝑛+1 −𝑝𝑛)2−𝑛∑n(pn+1−pn)2−n, and named the shape of the missing input as a sufficiently quantitative and uniform prime-tuples hypothesis giving statistical control of the binary expansion of about log⁡log⁡𝑛log⁡log⁡n consecutive gaps [23]. Theorem 4.3 below is that reduction in exact form, with the endpoint retained, with convergence supplied by an elementary bound, and with the statement checked by the Lean kernel. The elementary bound replaces the prime number theorem in this reduction.

A sufficiently uniform Hardy–Littlewood hypothesis gives conditional results of a different kind. Land’s draft states conditional irrationality [13]; Ringer’s draft states conditional normality in each integer base . The authors supply formalisation material, which has not been independently rebuilt for this revision. The uniform hypothesis in [12] controls growing tuples, with constants chosen before the tuple and basepoint; qualitative fixed-tuple Hardy–Littlewood does not provide it.

The version of Ringer’s source consulted on 16 September 2026 separates a stopped first-point comparison from this stronger conjecture. Its averaged one-sided tuple error is sufficient, and a bounded-domination condition on first-point masses is weaker still; these are alternative sufficient inputs, not conclusions of presently invoked unconditional prime-gap results. The signs matter: both an undercount at one parity of the truncation and an overcount at the other can be adverse. An upper sieve alone therefore does not supply that averaged input. None of these conditional inputs is assumed below.

Erdős stated on p. 93 of the 1958 article that ∑𝑛𝑝𝑘𝑛/𝑛!∑npnk/n! is irrational for every 𝑘 ≥1k≥1, and wrote there that the proof for 𝑘 >1k>1 is complicated enough that only the case 𝑘 =1k=1 is printed [1]. A proof of the full family appears in Schlage-Puchta’s Theorem 3, which gives the stronger statement that 1,𝑆0,𝑆1,𝑆2,…1,S0,S1,S2,… are linearly independent over ℚQ, where 𝑆𝑘 =∑𝑛≥1𝑝𝑘𝑛/𝑛!Sk=∑n≥1pnk/n! .

On page 103 of his 1988 problem paper Erdős separately stated the fixed-denominator problem: he could not prove that ∑𝑛𝑝𝑘𝑛/2𝑛∑npnk/2n is irrational for every 𝑘 ≥1k≥1, and wrote that the case 𝑘 =1k=1 was probably already very difficult. He also stated the variable-denominator expectation that ∑𝑛≥1𝑝𝑛/(𝑔1⋯𝑔𝑛)∑n≥1pn/(g1⋯gn) is irrational whenever 𝑔𝑛 ≥2gn≥2 and 𝑔𝑛 =𝑜(𝑝𝑛)gn=o(pn) [4]. That expectation is false: on 15 April 2026 Kovač posted a note, with the printed attribution ChatGPT 5.4 Pro (orchestrated by Vjeko Kovač), constructing such a sequence (𝑔𝑛)(gn) for which the sum is exactly 11 [24].

Section 3 of the 1958 article concerns variable product denominators, not the dyadic denominator sequence [1]. Its printed growth condition (5) uses nonstandard asymptotic typography; we do not use that condition as an operative hypothesis or silently translate it into a modern quantified statement. The simple endpoint example is unambiguous: if 𝐺𝑛 =∏𝑛𝑗=1(𝑝𝑗 +1)Gn=∏j=1n(pj+1) and 𝐺0 =1G0=1, then

𝑝𝑛𝐺𝑛=1𝐺𝑛−1−1𝐺𝑛,∑𝑛≥1𝑝𝑛𝐺𝑛=1.pnGn=1Gn−1−1Gn,∑n≥1pnGn=1.

Neither this variable-denominator example nor the counterexample in addresses fixed dyadic denominators.

There is also a genuinely adjacent proved dyadic theorem. If 𝑃(𝑚)P(m) denotes the largest prime factor of 𝑚m, Erdős and Pomerance proved that

∑𝑚≥2𝟏{𝑃(𝑚)>𝑃(𝑚+1)}2𝑚∑m≥21{P(m)>P(m+1)}2m

is irrational . Erdős and Graham record the complementary indicator on p. 62: equality of the two largest prime factors is impossible for consecutive integers, so its series is 1/21/2 minus the displayed one and is irrational as well. That is a theorem about a bounded prime-factor comparison digit sequence, and the numerators in ΠΠ are unbounded.

Two further results of Schlage-Puchta enter below. His Theorem 2 classifies rationality for numbers whose base-𝑏b digit string concatenates the representations of a slowly growing integer sequence, and is a different object from the tail criterion here; it was already pointed at this problem in the catalogue thread on 15 April 2026. His Lemma 4 is the input this note actually uses. It states that for every polynomial 𝐹 ∈ℤ[𝑥0,…,𝑥𝑘]F∈Z[x0,…,xk] which does not vanish identically, 𝐹(𝑔𝑛,…,𝑔𝑛+𝑘) ≠0F(gn,…,gn+k)≠0 for almost all 𝑛n, where 𝑔𝑛gn are the actual consecutive prime gaps [18]. Its proof runs through Selberg’s sieve. Sections 8 draws two consequences from it.

Theorems 8.1 and 2.1 fill intervals of attainable values. The first is a binary expansion. For the second, the direct reference is Crmarić–Kovač’s finite-choice covering lemma [27]: a menu’s largest successive gap must not exceed the total remaining diameter. They apply it to product-denominator series. Our menus are 𝑋𝑗 ={0,𝑤𝑗,…,𝐷𝑗𝑤𝑗}Xj={0,wj,…,Djwj}, so the hypothesis is 𝑤𝑗 ≤∑𝑖>𝑗𝐷𝑖𝑤𝑖wj≤∑i>jDiwi. Fridy’s generalised-base lemma [9] is an antecedent with nonincreasing weights; the finite-menu form avoids that additional assumption. Kovač–Tao use reciprocal menus [11], while van Doorn–Kovač combine filling with a divisibility chain absorbing every integer [20]. Our factorial moduli use the latter absorption property to preserve eventual congruences.

A further comparison is van Doorn’s exchange {21𝑑,28𝑑} ↔{20𝑑,30𝑑}{21d,28d}↔{20d,30d}: both reciprocal sums are 1/(12𝑑)1/(12d), while the ordinary sums are 49𝑑49d and 50𝑑50d [29]. Our paired corrections preserve the ordinary sum and vary the dyadic contribution instead. This is an analogy between conserved quantities, not an application of his partition theorem. We claim no new interval-covering principle.

Binary achievement sets require care beyond these covering inequalities. Bartoszewicz–Filipczak–Szymonik use a central run of attainable integer block sums to obtain interior in a multigeometric family [32]. Prus-Wiśniowski–Ptak construct Cantorvals for which the overlap indices {𝑛 :𝑎𝑛 ≤∑𝑖>𝑛𝑎𝑖}{n:an≤∑i>nai} have density zero [31]. Thus neither occasional separated cylinders nor failure of an eventual term-versus-tail alternative alone decides interior. The survey records the surrounding classification. Our variable-digit proof verifies covering at every stage and does not depend on a classification theorem for binary subsums. Nitecki’s preprint [36] gives an exposition explicitly crediting the Guthrie–Nymann classification; its title and numbering differ from the published Monthly article.

The inequality pattern alone is insufficient even when its index set is specified exactly: Marchwicki–Miska’s construction , with the repaired proof in [37], can realise any infinite strict term-dominating index set with a Cantor achievement set. The repair preserves the original uniqueness conclusion; the latter paper also gives a simpler proof of a weaker statement without uniqueness. Nowakowski’s Star Procedure [39] is a different sufficient route to a Cantorval, requiring every stage of a positivity recursion. None of these results is asserted to settle the prescribed factorial binary family in the separate working note.

Automatic sequences and the limit of the analogy.

Adamczewski–Drmota–Müllner prove computable logarithmic densities for fixed automatic sequences along primes, and give criteria for natural densities and their rationality [28]. The general logarithmic densities are not all rational. The fixed finite-alphabet automaton is essential: the result is not a theorem about unbounded consecutive prime gaps, their complete dyadic tails, or a growing family of residue or carry automata. Any such application would have to specify the automaton, prove that it computes the required observable, and supply uniform errors as its state space grows. We do not infer any of those steps from the density theorem.

The uniformity required from prime statistics.

Kuperberg’s large-set singular-series estimates allow a specified growing cardinality, not arbitrary dimension [12]. Her arithmetic-progression and smooth-weight estimates are a useful fixed-parameter comparison ; they do not by themselves give a law for ordered consecutive-gap blocks. Jha’s revised Poisson-tail preprint [34] concerns growing short-interval prime counts under a strong Hardy–Littlewood hypothesis. Counting primes in an interval and controlling the joint position-weighted gap-tail observable are different tasks. No growing-window estimate needed below is claimed to follow merely from these related titles or from a fixed-dimensional limit theorem.

Problem #251 also appears as the unproved declaration erdos_251 in the Formal Conjectures repository [25]. Its zero-based Lean sum starts with the zeroth prime over 2020, so it is twice the displayed normalisation and has equivalent irrationality status; its proof is sorry.

The strategy.

The digits 𝑝𝑛pn grow, so the series is not a digit expansion in any bounded alphabet, and the standard rationality criteria for such expansions do not apply directly. The classical elementary criteria for series of this kind instead control irrationality through the growth of the denominators. Erdős and Straus named a sum ∑𝑘1/𝑎𝑘∑k1/ak over a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers an Ahmes series [6]; for such a series the condition 𝑎1/2𝑘𝑘 →∞ak1/2k→∞ is sufficient for irrationality, and it is sharp, since shifted Sylvester sequences grow like 𝐶2𝑘C2k for arbitrarily large 𝐶C and have rational reciprocal sum. Both statements and their attribution are recorded in the introduction of Kovač and Tao [11]. Splitting each term 𝑝𝑖/2𝑖+1pi/2i+1 into 𝑝𝑖pi copies of 2−(𝑖+1)2−(i+1) writes ΠΠ as a sum of unit fractions with repetitions, and the denominators occurring in it are exactly the powers of two. Even ignoring the repetitions the growth hypothesis fails by every available margin, since (2𝑛)1/2𝑛 →1(2n)1/2n→1, and every arithmetic constraint has to come from the numerators instead.

What replaces growth control is denominator control on the sequence of rescaled tails. Rationality of the sum is equivalent to an eventual integrality condition on differences of those tails, and that condition uses nothing about the numerators beyond the fact that they are integers. The condition does not by itself force the numerators to repeat: Proposition 8.10, applied to 𝐾𝑛 =𝑛Kn=n, produces the integer sequence 𝜅𝑛 =𝑛 −1κn=n−1, which is unbounded and hence not eventually periodic, and whose dyadic sum is zero.

Dependencies and reading routes.

The sparse theorem is independent of primes: modular repair and finite-menu covering give the interval, and counting changed starts gives its statistical consequences. Schlage-Puchta’s lemma and the prime number theorem enter only the prime-anchored joint corollary. The recurrence classification needs integer digits and Euler’s congruence, not any prime-tuple conjecture. The one-tail certificate adds an explicit majorant and exact finite prime data. Irrationality would require the additional cofinal prime-gap input in Section 10. The appendices give the finite certificates, complete moved statements and source concordance. The accompanying statement-destination table preserves the original short-note labels at these locations.

Summation by parts, with the endpoint retained

Summation by parts trades a sequence for its consecutive differences. The form recorded here is exact: it carries no error term, it assumes nothing about the sequence, and it retains the endpoint term. No endpoint is absorbed into an estimate. For a sequence 𝑃P of rational numbers and 𝑛 ≥0n≥0 put

𝐷(𝑃,𝑛)=𝑛−1∑𝑖=0𝑃(𝑖)2𝑖+1,Δ(𝑃,𝑛)=𝑛−1∑𝑖=0𝑃(𝑖+1)−𝑃(𝑖)2𝑖+1,D(P,n)=∑i=0n−1P(i)2i+1,Δ(P,n)=∑i=0n−1P(i+1)−P(i)2i+1,

both empty, hence zero, at 𝑛 =0n=0. We call these the dyadic partial sum and the dyadic difference sum of 𝑃P.

Proposition 4.1 (finite summation by parts). For every rational sequence 𝑃P and every 𝑛 ≥0n≥0,

𝐷(𝑃,𝑛+1)=𝑃(0)+Δ(𝑃,𝑛)−𝑃(𝑛)2𝑛+1.D(P,n+1)=P(0)+Δ(P,n)−P(n)2n+1.

Proof. A routine induction on 𝑛n. At 𝑛 =0n=0 both sides equal 𝑃(0)/2P(0)/2. For the step, adding 𝑃(𝑛 +1)/2𝑛+2P(n+1)/2n+2 to the left and (𝑃(𝑛 +1) −𝑃(𝑛))/2𝑛+1(P(n+1)−P(n))/2n+1 to the difference sum changes the endpoint term from 𝑃(𝑛)/2𝑛+1P(n)/2n+1 to 𝑃(𝑛 +1)/2𝑛+2P(n+1)/2n+2, and the two adjustments agree. ◻

Formalised as the summation-by-parts identity. Nothing is assumed about 𝑃P: no positivity, no monotonicity, and no convergence.

Specialising to 𝑃(𝑖) =𝑝𝑖P(i)=pi, whose first value is 𝑝0 =2p0=2, and writing 𝑔𝑖 =𝑝𝑖+1 −𝑝𝑖gi=pi+1−pi for the zero-based gaps, gives the reformulation.

Theorem 4.2 (prime-gap reformulation). Let 𝑝0 =2,𝑝1 =3,…p0=2,p1=3,… be the primes in increasing order and 𝑔𝑖 =𝑝𝑖+1 −𝑝𝑖gi=pi+1−pi. For every 𝑛 ≥0n≥0,

𝑛∑𝑖=0𝑝𝑖2𝑖+1=2+𝑛−1∑𝑖=0𝑔𝑖2𝑖+1−𝑝𝑛2𝑛+1.∑i=0npi2i+1=2+∑i=0n−1gi2i+1−pn2n+1.

Formalised as the prime-gap summation by parts, using the gap partial sum and the gap cast identity; the latter records that the natural-number difference 𝑝𝑛+1 −𝑝𝑛pn+1−pn agrees with the difference taken in ℚQ, which needs 𝑝𝑛 ≤𝑝𝑛+1pn≤pn+1, the monotonicity step. The leading 22 is the first prime, not a normalising constant. At 𝑛 =2n=2, for instance, the left side is 2/2 +3/4 +5/8 =19/82/2+3/4+5/8=19/8 and the right side is 2 +(1/2 +2/4) −5/8 =19/82+(1/2+2/4)−5/8=19/8.

The infinite identity and the irrationality equivalence

Write

𝑢𝑛=𝑝𝑛2𝑛+1,𝑣𝑛=𝑔𝑛2𝑛+1un=pn2n+1,vn=gn2n+1

for the terms of the prime series and of the gap series, so that ∑𝑛≥0𝑢𝑛 =Π∑n≥0un=Π. The termwise identity 𝑣𝑛 =2𝑢𝑛+1 −𝑢𝑛vn=2un+1−un is the dyadic discrete derivative. It expresses each gap term as an integer combination of two consecutive prime terms, so once (𝑢𝑛)(un) is summable the gap series can be summed by rearranging two copies of the prime series.

Theorem 4.3 (infinite prime-gap identity). Both series converge and

∑𝑛≥0𝑝𝑛2𝑛+1=2+∑𝑛≥0𝑔𝑛2𝑛+1.∑n≥0pn2n+1=2+∑n≥0gn2n+1.

Proof. The bound 𝑝𝑛 ≤1250(𝑛 +1)4pn≤1250(n+1)4 of Appendix A makes (𝑢𝑛)(un) summable, and 0 <𝑔𝑛 ≤𝑝𝑛+10<gn≤pn+1 then makes (𝑣𝑛)(vn) summable. The shifted sequence (𝑢𝑛+1)(un+1) is summable, so summing 𝑣𝑛 =2𝑢𝑛+1 −𝑢𝑛vn=2un+1−un and using 𝑢0 =1u0=1 gives

∑𝑛≥0𝑣𝑛=2(∑𝑛≥0𝑢𝑛−𝑢0)−∑𝑛≥0𝑢𝑛=∑𝑛≥0𝑢𝑛−2.◻∑n≥0vn=2(∑n≥0un−u0)−∑n≥0un=∑n≥0un−2.◻

◻

The polynomial bound is checked here, summability of the prime series here, the summability transfer is the gap-series summability theorem, and the displayed identity is the unconditional prime-gap identity. The prime number theorem is needed neither for this convergence nor for the identity; it enters later through 𝑝𝑛 ∼𝑛log⁡𝑛pn∼nlog⁡n in Corollary 8.4 and in the state-compression argument [17].

Corollary 4.4 (exact irrationality reformulation). ΠΠ is irrational if and only if 𝑆 =∑𝑛≥0𝑔𝑛2−(𝑛+1)S=∑n≥0gn2−(n+1) is irrational. The corresponding zero-based series with denominator 2𝑛2n equals 4 +2𝑆4+2S and has the same irrationality status.

These are the normalised irrationality equivalence, the displayed-series identity, and the displayed-series irrationality equivalence. Concretely, Π =3.674643966…Π=3.674643966… is irrational if and only if 𝑆 =1.674643966…S=1.674643966… is, and neither is known.

The tail recurrence and the exact criteria

The series is not attacked directly. Suppose ∑𝑖≥0𝑎𝑖2−(𝑖+1)∑i≥0ai2−(i+1) converges with every 𝑎𝑖ai an integer, and rescale its tails by putting

𝑇𝑁=2𝑁+1∑𝑖>𝑁𝑎𝑖2𝑖+1=∑𝑗≥1𝑎𝑁+𝑗2𝑗.TN=2N+1∑i>Nai2i+1=∑j≥1aN+j2j.

Two facts follow immediately. First 𝑇𝑁+1 =2𝑇𝑁 −𝑎𝑁+1TN+1=2TN−aN+1, so moving one level along doubles the rescaled tail and subtracts a single coefficient. Second 𝑇0 =2∑𝑖≥0𝑎𝑖2−(𝑖+1) −𝑎0T0=2∑i≥0ai2−(i+1)−a0, so the sum is rational exactly when 𝑇0T0 is. This section studies that recurrence, assuming nothing about the coefficients beyond the fact that they are integers, and resumes the prime-gap instance at the end.

Definition 5.1. Let 𝑔 :ℕ →ℤg:N→Z and 𝑇 :ℕ →ℚT:N→Q or 𝑇 :ℕ →ℝT:N→R. Say 𝑇T satisfies the dyadic tail recurrence with digits 𝑔g when 𝑇𝑁+1 =2𝑇𝑁 −𝑔𝑁+1TN+1=2TN−gN+1 for every 𝑁N. Write 𝜎ℎ(𝑁) =𝑇𝑁+ℎ −𝑇𝑁σh(N)=TN+h−TN for the shift of length ℎh at 𝑁N, and call a rational number integral when it is the image of an integer.

These are the tail recurrence, the shift, and integrality. One small orbit is worth having in view. Take every digit 𝑔𝑁 =0gN=0 and 𝑇0 =1/12T0=1/12. Then the orbit is 112,16,13,23,43,…112,16,13,23,43,… and 𝜎ℎ(𝑁) =(2ℎ −1)2𝑁/12σh(N)=(2h−1)2N/12. The shift of length 22 is not integral at 𝑁 =0N=0 and is integral at 𝑁 =2N=2; the shift of length 11 is never integral. Nonintegrality at one prescribed shift length therefore does not imply irrationality.

Iterating the recurrence ℎh times multiplies 𝑇𝑁TN by 2ℎ2h and accumulates an explicit integer. Define 𝐵0,𝑁 =0B0,N=0 and 𝐵ℎ+1,𝑁 =2𝐵ℎ,𝑁 +𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1Bh+1,N=2Bh,N+gN+h+1, so that 𝐵ℎ,𝑁 =𝑔𝑁+12ℎ−1 +⋯ +𝑔𝑁+ℎBh,N=gN+12h−1+⋯+gN+h: the tail block.

Theorem 5.2 (block identity). For every 𝑁N and ℎh,

𝑇𝑁+ℎ=2ℎ𝑇𝑁−𝐵ℎ,𝑁,hence𝜎ℎ(𝑁)=(2ℎ−1)𝑇𝑁−𝐵ℎ,𝑁.TN+h=2hTN−Bh,N,henceσh(N)=(2h−1)TN−Bh,N.

Proof. A routine induction on ℎh; the step is one application of the recurrence together with the recursion defining 𝐵B. The second identity is the first minus 𝑇𝑁TN. ◻

Formalised as the iterated block identity and the scaled shift identity. The shift also obeys the recurrence in its own right,

𝜎ℎ(𝑁+1)=2𝜎ℎ(𝑁)−(𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1−𝑔𝑁+1),(5)(5)σh(N+1)=2σh(N)−(gN+h+1−gN+1),

the shift step identity. Since 𝐵ℎ,𝑁Bh,N is an integer, Theorem 5.2 converts a question about the shift into a question about (2ℎ −1)𝑇𝑁(2h−1)TN: the shift 𝜎ℎ(𝑁)σh(N) is integral if and only if (2ℎ −1)𝑇𝑁(2h−1)TN is, the integral-shift criterion. The criterion holds in both directions, so once 𝑇𝑁TN is fixed no choice of the digits after index 𝑁N can change whether 𝜎ℎ(𝑁)σh(N) is an integer.

For a rational orbit the denominator settles the matter exactly:

den⁡(𝑇𝑁+1)=den⁡(𝑇𝑁)gcd(2,den⁡(𝑇𝑁)),𝜎ℎ(𝑁)∈ℤ⟺den⁡(𝑇𝑁)∣2ℎ−1.(6)(6)den⁡(TN+1)=den⁡(TN)gcd(2,den⁡(TN)),σh(N)∈Z⟺den⁡(TN)∣2h−1.

Each even denominator loses exactly one factor of 22 and an odd denominator is unchanged, so after finitely many steps the denominator is an odd integer 𝑑d; Euler’s congruence then gives 𝑑 ∣2𝜑(𝑑) −1d∣2φ(d)−1, and the multiplicative order of 22 modulo 𝑑d is the least such exponent. These are the denominator recurrence, its odd case and even case, the denominator classification, the totient shift, and the propagation of an integral shift to every later index. The hypothesis that 𝑑d is odd cannot be dropped: if 𝑇𝑁 =1/2TN=1/2 then 2ℎ −12h−1 is odd for every ℎ ≥1h≥1, so no shift at 𝑁N is integral.

Theorem 5.3 (exact rationality classification). Let 𝑇 :ℕ →ℝT:N→R satisfy 𝑇𝑁+1 =2𝑇𝑁 −𝑔𝑁+1TN+1=2TN−gN+1 with integer digits 𝑔g. The following are equivalent:

  1. 𝑇0T0 is rational;

  2. 𝜎ℎ(𝑁)σh(N) is an integer for some ℎ ≥1h≥1 and some 𝑁N;

  3. for some fixed ℎ ≥1h≥1, 𝜎ℎ(𝑁)σh(N) is an integer at every sufficiently large 𝑁N.

Consequently 𝑇0T0 is irrational if and only if every positive-length shift is nonintegral at every index, equivalently if and only if for every ℎ ≥1h≥1 and every cutoff some later 𝑁N has 𝜎ℎ(𝑁) ∉ℤσh(N)∉Z.

Proof. For (i)⇒⇒(iii), the block identity identifies the whole orbit with a rational recurrence starting at 𝑇0T0; apply (6) at an index where the denominator has become odd, and propagate forward. The implication (iii)⇒⇒(ii) is immediate. For (ii)⇒⇒(i), the block identity gives 𝜎ℎ(𝑁) =(2ℎ −1)𝑇𝑁 −𝐵ℎ,𝑁σh(N)=(2h−1)TN−Bh,N with 𝐵ℎ,𝑁Bh,N and 𝜎ℎ(𝑁)σh(N) integers and 2ℎ −1 ≠02h−1≠0, so 𝑇𝑁TN is rational, and 𝑇𝑁 =2𝑁𝑇0 −𝐵𝑁,0TN=2NT0−BN,0 then makes 𝑇0T0 rational. Negating the three conditions gives the two irrationality formulations. ◻

The exact real classifiers are one integral positive shift, eventual integrality, pointwise nonintegrality, and cofinal nonintegrality.

Lemma 5.4 (the boundary condition identifying a true tail). Let 𝑎1,𝑎2,…a1,a2,… be real numbers with ∑𝑗≥1|𝑎𝑗|2−𝑗 <∞∑j≥1|aj|2−j<∞, and let 𝑈𝑁+1 =2𝑈𝑁 −𝑎𝑁+1UN+1=2UN−aN+1. Then

𝑈𝑁=∑𝑗≥1𝑎𝑁+𝑗2−𝑗for every 𝑁⟺2−𝑁𝑈𝑁⟶0.UN=∑j≥1aN+j2−jfor every N⟺2−NUN⟶0.

Proof. Iteration gives 2−𝑁𝑈𝑁 =𝑈0 −∑𝑁𝑗=1𝑎𝑗2−𝑗2−NUN=U0−∑j=1Naj2−j. The limit is zero exactly when 𝑈0U0 equals the full series; subtracting its first 𝑁N terms then gives the claimed tail formula. In particular, the recurrence alone leaves the homogeneous freedom 𝐶2𝑁C2N. ◻

The actual prime-gap orbit.

Put

𝑇𝑁=∑𝑗≥1𝑔𝑁+𝑗2𝑗,TN=∑j≥1gN+j2j,

which converges by Theorem 4.3. The scaled tail equals its shifted-gap series, the shifted-gap series identity, and satisfies 𝑇𝑁+1 =2𝑇𝑁 −𝑔𝑁+1TN+1=2TN−gN+1 with no rationality hypothesis, the real tail recurrence. Since 𝑇0 =2𝑆 −1 =2.349287932…T0=2S−1=2.349287932…, the numbers ΠΠ, 𝑆S and 𝑇0T0 have the same rationality status, and Theorem 5.3 specialises to the actual series: irrationality of ΠΠ is equivalent to cofinal nonintegrality of the positive shifts of 𝑇T, the escape equivalence. Nothing about the bridge from the series to its actual tail is left open; the open content is the escape hypothesis itself.

The free-pair criterion and the lcm diagonal

The escape condition quantifies over a fixed shift length. Freeing the offset gives an equivalent condition with a weaker-looking producer.

Theorem 5.5 (free-pair criterion). 𝑆S is irrational if and only if for every 𝑡 ≥1t≥1 and every 𝑁0N0 there are 𝑁,𝑀 ≥𝑁0N,M≥N0 with 𝑀 ≡𝑁(mod𝑡)M≡N(modt) and 𝑇𝑀 −𝑇𝑁 ∉ℤTM−TN∉Z.

Proof. If 𝑆S is irrational, take 𝑀 =𝑁 +𝑡M=N+t for the 𝑁N supplied by Theorem 5.3 at shift length 𝑡t. Conversely, suppose 𝑆S is rational. By (6) the orbit reaches an index 𝑁0N0 beyond which the reduced denominator is a fixed odd 𝑑d; let 𝑡t be the multiplicative order of 22 modulo 𝑑d. For 𝑁,𝑀 ≥𝑁0N,M≥N0 with 𝑀 ≡𝑁M≡N modulo 𝑡t, the difference 𝑇𝑀 −𝑇𝑁TM−TN is then an integer, contradicting the stated property at this 𝑡t and this cutoff. ◻

The offset 𝑀 −𝑁M−N is free, so one nonintegral congruent pair for each modulus and each cutoff suffices in place of a supply at a single fixed offset. The mechanism is exact: beyond a rational state with odd reduced denominator 𝑑d, the difference 𝑇𝑀 −𝑇𝑁TM−TN is integral precisely when 𝑀 ≡𝑁M≡N modulo the order of 22 in ℤ/𝑑ℤZ/dZ, the free-pair lattice, so every rational orbit has a cutoff and a modulus at which integrality holds exactly on the congruence classes, the lattice corollary. The criterion for the actual series is checked as the free-pair equivalence, over the actual real tail recurrence. The mechanism is elementary: modulo one the tail recurrence is multiplication by two, and integrality of 𝑇𝑀 −𝑇𝑁TM−TN beyond a rational state is governed by the multiplicative order of 22 modulo the odd reduced denominator.

The criterion rules out two shortcuts. For the actual prime-gap tail, Section D.4 combines the prime number theorem with a first-moment bound to show that, under rationality, some tail value occurs ≫𝐶,𝑑𝑋/log⁡𝑋≫C,dX/log⁡X times in (𝑋,2𝑋](X,2X]; here 𝑑d is the eventual odd reduced denominator and 𝐶 >1C>1 is fixed. This is specific to the prime tail, rather than a consequence of rationality for arbitrary integer-digit orbits, and equal tails have integral difference, so they do not supply the free-pair producer. Also, under the free-pair lattice the difference is an integer whenever the modulus divides the offset, and an integer cannot lie in (12,1)(12,1), so the window component of the reduced event below is already a contradiction on its own. Both derivations are ordinary proofs, recorded in the extended record and not formalised.

A second exact reformulation collapses all shift lengths and basepoints onto a single schedule. Let 𝐿0 =1L0=1 and 𝐿𝑗 =lcm⁡(1,…,𝑗)Lj=lcm⁡(1,…,j).

The factorial schedule has the same divisibility property; the lcm schedule is pointwise no larger and is the endpoint used here. Theorems 5.5 and 5.6 are exact reformulations on the class of integer-digit orbits. They change the shape of the required producer and they supply no nonintegrality statement for the actual prime gaps.

A local certificate, and one actual pair

The classifiers reduce irrationality to a condition of infinite precision imposed on a complete tail. Inside ( −1,1)(−1,1) integrality is equality with zero, so on that range the shift step identity (5) turns simultaneous integrality of two adjacent shifts into a single comparison of digits. What this buys is a certificate attached to one pair of adjacent indices, whose verification already contradicts integrality there. The distance of a shift from the integers never has to be estimated.

What is missing is the pair of inequalities, each of which constrains a complete infinite tail.

What cannot supply the missing input

The counterexamples in this section test which information about the gaps could force irrationality. They preserve selected growth, residue and nonconcentration properties while changing the dyadic value. The sparsity result has a different role: it rules out a positive-proportion lower bound for the two-window event, while leaving sparse-witness arguments available.

Bounded residue-preserving perturbations

Theorem 8.1 (bounded-perturbation obstruction). Let 𝑎𝑛an be natural numbers with ∑𝑛≥0𝑎𝑛2−(𝑛+1)∑n≥0an2−(n+1) convergent. For every integer 𝑀 ≥1M≥1 and every cutoff 𝐾K there are digits 𝜀𝑛 ∈{0,1}εn∈{0,1}, zero for 𝑛 <𝐾n<K, such that ∑𝑛≥0(𝑎𝑛 +𝑀𝜀𝑛)2−(𝑛+1)∑n≥0(an+Mεn)2−(n+1) is rational.

The construction is kernel checked. The invariant-property consequence—a property shared by every admissible perturbation cannot by itself force irrationality—is the ordinary logical reading of that construction, rather than a separately named Lean theorem. The construction is also checked at the actual consecutive prime gaps for every 𝑀 ≥1M≥1 and every 𝐾K, the rational perturbed prime-gap series, with the perturbed gap lying in [𝑔𝑛,𝑔𝑛 +𝑀][gn,gn+M] and congruent to 𝑔𝑛gn modulo 𝑀M, the gap bounds. Consequently no theorem about the size or the residue of prime gaps that survives such a perturbation can suffice for Problem #251; that class includes the bounded-gap and large-gap theorems cited in Section 10 and equidistribution of 𝑝𝑛pn modulo any fixed 𝑞q, on taking 𝑀 =2𝑞M=2q. The perturbed digits need not remain prime gaps.

Algebraic nonconcentration survives the rationalising perturbation

Fixed-block polynomial nonconcentration is a finer property than size and residue, but it too survives the bounded perturbation. The relevant input is Schlage-Puchta’s Lemma 4: for every polynomial 𝐹 ∈ℤ[𝑥0,…,𝑥𝑘]F∈Z[x0,…,xk] which does not vanish identically, 𝐹(𝑔𝑛,…,𝑔𝑛+𝑘) ≠0F(gn,…,gn+k)≠0 for almost all 𝑛n [18]. Say that an integer sequence 𝑎a has fixed-block nonconcentration when it satisfies that conclusion for every 𝑘 ≥0k≥0 and every nonzero 𝐹 ∈ℤ[𝑥0,…,𝑥𝑘]F∈Z[x0,…,xk]. The property transfers across bounded perturbations with no independence or randomness assumption.

The displayed finite shifted-count bound is unconditional by the ordinary proof above. Its historical source locator is not present in the supplied declaration index, so no checked-build status is assigned to that link here. To deduce zero density one still needs, for every 𝜀 >0ε>0 and all large 𝑁N, a choice of 𝐻H making the right side less than 𝜀𝑁(𝐻 +1)εN(H+1). The adjacent case ℎ =1h=1 instead requires the corresponding three-prime estimate, because two of the four positions would coincide. The all-shift implication records these analytic premises explicitly; it supplies neither estimate and does not prove irrationality.

Theorem 8.3 (nonconcentration is perturbation-stable). Let 𝑎 :ℕ →ℤa:N→Z have fixed-block nonconcentration, let 𝐸 ⊂ℤE⊂Z be finite, and let 𝑏𝑛 =𝑎𝑛 +𝑒𝑛bn=an+en with 𝑒𝑛 ∈𝐸en∈E for every 𝑛n. Then 𝑏b has fixed-block nonconcentration.

{𝑛:𝐹(𝑏𝑛,…,𝑏𝑛+𝑘)=0}⊆⋃𝐞∈𝐸𝑘+1{𝑛:𝐹𝐞(𝑎𝑛,…,𝑎𝑛+𝑘)=0}.{n:F(bn,…,bn+k)=0}⊆⋃e∈Ek+1{n:Fe(an,…,an+k)=0}.

These are ordinary deductions from the sparse theorem and the stated external analytic input. The reconstructed positions need not be prime. Neither a bounded translation nor a sparse change preserves general relative frequencies of rare events; their two transfer arguments have different hypotheses and must not be conflated.

The two-window event has density zero

The same lemma bounds the event that the local certificate consumes.

Theorem 8.7 (sparsity of the two-window event). Fix ℎ ≥1h≥1. The set of 𝑁 ≥1N≥1 at which the three hypotheses of Theorem 6.1 hold for the actual prime gaps has density zero. For the same ℎh, the set of 𝑁N with 𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1 =𝑔𝑁+1gN+h+1=gN+1 also has density zero.

Proof. For 𝑁 ≥1N≥1 every gap involved is even, so 𝛿𝑁 =𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1 −𝑔𝑁+1δN=gN+h+1−gN+1 is even. If |𝜎ℎ(𝑁)| <1|σh(N)|<1, |𝜎ℎ(𝑁 +1)| <1|σh(N+1)|<1 and 𝛿𝑁 ≠0δN≠0, then 𝛿𝑁 =2𝜎ℎ(𝑁) −𝜎ℎ(𝑁 +1)δN=2σh(N)−σh(N+1) lies in ( −3,3)(−3,3), so 𝛿𝑁 = ±2δN=±2. Apply Schlage-Puchta’s lemma [18] at index 𝑛 =𝑁 +1n=N+1 with 𝑘 =ℎk=h to the two polynomials 𝐹±(𝑥0,…,𝑥ℎ) =𝑥ℎ −𝑥0 ∓2F±(x0,…,xh)=xh−x0∓2, neither of which vanishes identically: each of {𝑁 :𝛿𝑁 =2}{N:δN=2} and {𝑁 :𝛿𝑁 = −2}{N:δN=−2} has density zero, and the event is contained in their union. The second assertion is the same lemma applied to 𝐹(𝑥0,…,𝑥ℎ) =𝑥ℎ −𝑥0F(x0,…,xh)=xh−x0. ◻

The two halves point in opposite directions and both are useful. The mismatch hypothesis on its own holds for almost all 𝑁N, which is strictly stronger than the cofinal statement Proposition 6.3 supplies. The full conjunction is confined to a set of density zero, because the two window conditions force the mismatch to be exactly ±2±2. A producer for Problem 10.2 therefore has to be a cofinality statement about a sparse set. Consequently, this event cannot be supplied on a set of positive lower density. A sufficient producer would have to yield cofinally many witnesses in a density-zero set; density zero alone does not exclude an averaging argument capable of detecting such sparse witnesses. The finite measurements in Section 9 show a decline across the sampled bands. They establish neither an asymptotic rate for the density nor a counting law. Prime-height cutoffs and gap-index cutoffs must also be distinguished before comparing any proposed rates.

Recurring gap values differing by two do not suffice

Theorem 6.4 reduces the producer to a ±2±2 mismatch together with a half-window condition. It is tempting to hope that the mismatch half is the substance, and that two even values differing by 22, each occurring infinitely often as a consecutive prime gap inside a common index residue class, would suffice. At the level of integer-digit recurrences that implication is false, and it stays false under growth at the scale the primes actually have.

The factorial schedule above proves recurrence in the zero residue class. The following separate construction strengthens this to every residue class.

A complete countermodel in every residue class

are integers, 𝑈0 =6U0=6, and 𝑈𝑁+ℎ −𝑈𝑁 ∈ℤUN+h−UN∈Z for every 𝑁,ℎ ≥0N,h≥0. The sequence

To obtain every residue class, enumerate triples consisting of a positive modulus, a residue, and a repetition index. Choose the corresponding centres 𝑐𝑘ck in the prescribed classes with 𝑐0 ≥100c0≥100, 𝑐𝑘+1 ≥𝑐𝑘 +3ck+1≥ck+3 and 𝑐𝑘 ≥2𝑘2ck≥2k2 for 𝑘 ≥1k≥1. The full statement is kernel-checked in Lean.

This rules out an inference from these coefficient properties alone to nonintegral tail shifts. It gives no counterexample to the prime-gap problem and does not reproduce the extreme large gaps of the primes.

The consequence is exact. Positivity, evenness, unboundedness, non-eventual periodicity, a pointwise logarithmic bound, cumulative growth at the prime-number-theorem scale, and the recurrence of two even values differing by 22 inside every index residue class are jointly compatible with an integral tail at every index. Any route through that input must use a property of the consecutive primes beyond this list. The sequence (𝑎𝑛)(an) is synthetic and the 𝑃𝑛Pn are not asserted to be prime. The pointwise logarithmic bound also precludes the known large-gap behaviour, so the theorem does not speak to hypotheses that use extreme gaps.

Proposition 8.9 (quadratic polynomial-shift countermodel). Put 𝑐𝑛 =2(𝑛2 +4𝑛 +2)cn=2(n2+4n+2) and 𝑈𝑛 =2(𝑛 +4)2Un=2(n+4)2. Then 𝑐𝑛cn is positive, even and strictly increasing, 𝑈𝑛+1 =2𝑈𝑛 −𝑐𝑛+1Un+1=2Un−cn+1, every shift 𝑈𝑁+ℎ −𝑈𝑁UN+h−UN is integral, 𝑐𝑛+1 −𝑐𝑛 =4𝑛 +10cn+1−cn=4n+10 is never ±2±2, and

∑𝑗≥1𝑐𝑗2𝑗=32.∑j≥1cj2j=32.

Proof. Direct expansion gives the recurrence, and the finite telescope is ∑𝑛𝑗=1𝑐𝑗2−𝑗 =32 −2(𝑛 +4)22−𝑛∑j=1ncj2−j=32−2(n+4)22−n, whose last term tends to zero. The remaining assertions follow from the integer values of 𝑈𝑛Un and from 𝑐𝑛+1 −𝑐𝑛 =4𝑛 +10 ≥10cn+1−cn=4n+10≥10. ◻

The series is the one starting at 𝑗 =1j=1, whose initial tail state is 𝑈0 =32U0=32; under the opening convention ∑𝑛≥0𝑐𝑛2−(𝑛+1)∑n≥0cn2−(n+1) the same word has value 1818, and the two ranges must be kept apart. The formal construction checks the recurrence, strict growth, integrality of every shift, exclusion of adjacent differences of size two, and the value 3232 for the shifted series, whose summand is 𝑐𝑛+1/2𝑛+1cn+1/2n+1; the rational value is recorded at line 109. Positivity, parity, strict growth, unboundedness and nonperiodicity are therefore jointly compatible with rationality, and the adjacent trigger of Theorem 6.4 fails at every index. The telescoping mechanism is the one used in the note of ChatGPT 5.4 Pro (orchestrated by Vjeko Kovač) against the variable-denominator expectation of Erdős [24]; the word is not a result about Problem #251.

Rationality also fails to force the coefficients to repeat. Let 𝐾 :ℕ →ℚK:N→Q be arbitrary and put 𝜅𝑛 =2𝐾𝑛 −𝐾𝑛+1κn=2Kn−Kn+1: the carry coefficient.

Proposition 8.10 (exact telescoping). For every 𝑛 ≥0n≥0, ∑𝑛−1𝑖=0𝜅𝑖2−(𝑖+1) =𝐾0 −𝐾𝑛2−𝑛∑i=0n−1κi2−(i+1)=K0−Kn2−n.

Proof. A routine induction; the added term is (2𝐾𝑛 −𝐾𝑛+1)2−(𝑛+1) =𝐾𝑛2−𝑛 −𝐾𝑛+12−(𝑛+1)(2Kn−Kn+1)2−(n+1)=Kn2−n−Kn+12−(n+1). ◻

The carry form 𝜅𝑛 =2𝐾𝑛 −𝐾𝑛+1κn=2Kn−Kn+1 is the case 𝑎𝑛 =2an=2 of the rationality criterion of Erdős and Straus: for integers 𝑏𝑛bn and positive integers 𝑎𝑛an with 𝑎𝑛 >1an>1 for all large 𝑛n and |𝑏𝑛|/(𝑎𝑛−1𝑎𝑛) →0|bn|/(an−1an)→0, the series ∑𝑛𝑏𝑛/(𝑎1⋯𝑎𝑛)∑nbn/(a1⋯an) is rational exactly when some positive integer 𝐵B and integers 𝑐𝑛cn satisfy 𝐵𝑏𝑛 =𝑐𝑛𝑎𝑛 −𝑐𝑛+1Bbn=cnan−cn+1 and |𝑐𝑛+1| <𝑎𝑛/2|cn+1|<an/2 for all large 𝑛n [7]. For the prime gaps the numerators 𝑏𝑛 =𝑔𝑛bn=gn are unbounded, so that hypothesis fails, and the proposition above imposes no condition on 𝐾K.

Formalised as the carry telescoping identity. Taking 𝐾0 =52K0=52 and 𝐾𝑛 =2𝑛 +2Kn=2n+2 for 𝑛 ≥1n≥1 gives 𝜅0 =1κ0=1 and 𝜅𝑛 =2𝑛κn=2n, so the coefficients 1,2,4,6,8,…1,2,4,6,8,… are positive, even after the first term, unbounded and not eventually periodic, while their dyadic sum is 5252. Rationality alone therefore cannot imply eventual periodicity even for a positive, parity-correct integer coefficient sequence, and no argument may play periodicity of a rational value against Proposition 6.3.

The affine and fixed-lattice escape formulations do not create new prime-distribution information. Their full definitions and exact hypotheses are preserved in Appendix E.

What is measured

Two finite computations report on the two producers. Each covers one bounded range and supplies no cofinal statement.

Over the 6 841 6486841648 primes below 1.2 ×1081.2×108 and offsets ℎ =1,…,16h=1,…,16, the reduced two-window event of Theorem 6.4 occurs at every offset, with density between 0.004180.00418 and 0.0082480.008248 and the two signs near balanced; at ℎ =1h=1 there are 56 42756427 occurrences among 6 841 5646841564 candidate indices, the last at the prime 119 995 753119995753. Rescaled by log⁡𝑝log⁡p the band densities run from 0.176710.17671 down to 0.131480.13148 with decelerating drift over the measured bands. This finite observation does not establish an asymptotic counting law or cofinality. The tails in this scan are double-precision floating-point, so an individual hit is a numerical observation and carries no certificate; the median distance from the shift to the nearer window boundary is 0.1270.127 and the worst case over 34 00034000 hits is 6.1 ×10−76.1×10−7, eight orders above the working resolution, and 3 2003200 sampled hits across ℎ =1,…,8h=1,…,8 were rechecked against the literal three-part statement with no violations. Proposition 6.6 is the one pair certified by exact integer arithmetic. The receipt is adjacent-mismatch.json.

Over the 1 270 6071270607 primes below 2 ×1072×107, and for every modulus 𝑡 ≤20t≤20 and every residue class modulo 𝑡t, the free-pair event of Theorem 5.5 has witnesses running to the last usable index: the leanest class at 𝑡 =20t=20 carries 90 15090150 witnesses and the latest witness sits at index 1 270 5201270520 of 1 270 5401270540. The recorded floating-point witnesses pass the stronger two-window test over this finite range; they are numerical observations, not exact certificates or a proof of either cofinal producer. What the scan does not supply is uniformity in 𝑡t and in the cutoff. The receipt is free-pair.json. The public computation guide provides the programs, dependencies and exact replay commands for all three recorded runs, including the continued-fraction calculation above.

The remaining obligation

Problem #251 is open. The exact unresolved condition, equivalent to irrationality by Theorem 5.3 and the escape equivalence for the actual tail, is the following.

Problem 10.1 (universal prime-gap shift escape). For every ℎ ≥1h≥1 and every 𝑁0N0, prove that some 𝑁 ≥𝑁0N≥N0 satisfies

∑𝑗≥1𝑔𝑁+ℎ+𝑗−𝑔𝑁+𝑗2𝑗∉ℤ.(7)(7)∑j≥1gN+h+j−gN+j2j∉Z.

Problem 10.2 (cofinal adjacent small mismatch). For every ℎ ≥1h≥1 and every 𝑁0N0, prove that some 𝑁 ≥𝑁0N≥N0 satisfies

| | |𝜎ℎ(𝑁)| | |<1,| | |𝜎ℎ(𝑁+1)| | |<1,𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1≠𝑔𝑁+1.(8)(8)|σh(N)|<1,|σh(N+1)|<1,gN+h+1≠gN+1.

Corollary 6.2 makes Problem 10.2 sufficient for Problem 10.1, and Theorem 5.5 supplies an equivalent target in which the offset is free. The three formulations are equivalent or ordered by implication; none of them is an analytic saving on its own.

What the proved obstructions leave. By Theorem 8.1 no hypothesis stable under bounded residue-preserving perturbation can work; by Corollary 8.4 adding fixed-block polynomial nonconcentration to that list does not repair it; the construction in Section 8.5 shows that recurring gap values differing by 22 in every residue class do not work at the level of integer recurrences; and by Theorem 8.7 the event in (8) has density zero, so it must be produced cofinally on a sparse set. Isolated small gaps, isolated large gaps and average gap estimates are insufficient. Any prescribed finite prefix can be preserved while the complete sum is rationalised, so that prefix alone cannot force irrationality or a cofinal small-tail producer. A finite block together with a proved tail bound can still certify one window: both inequalities in (8) contain the complete infinite continuation, and Proposition 6.5 supplies the corresponding finite reduction. Nor does parity help, since after the first gap every 𝑔𝑛gn is even.

The finite reduction is available. Proposition 6.5 turns each window condition into an integer comparison at truncation length 𝐿L, and for fixed ℎh and 𝜀 >0ε>0 the choice 𝐿 =⌈(4 +𝜀)log2⁡(𝑁 +2)⌉L=⌈(4+ε)log2⁡(N+2)⌉ makes 𝐸ℎ,𝑁,𝐿 =𝑂ℎ(𝑁−𝜀)Eh,N,L=Oh(N−ε). A prescribed positive margin 𝜂ℎηh therefore converts (8) into the stronger task of producing the corresponding fixed-margin finite-block events. Strict open-window membership alone need not supply such a fixed margin. The finite event concerns the joint distribution modulo powers of two of the block (𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1 −𝑔𝑁+1,…,𝑔𝑁+ℎ+𝐿 −𝑔𝑁+𝐿)(gN+h+1−gN+1,…,gN+h+L−gN+L) over a window of logarithmic length. Deciding one instance costs 𝑂(log⁡𝑁)O(log⁡N) gaps together with the elementary prime bound; producing certified witnesses beyond every cutoff, for each fixed ℎh, is the unproved input. Uniform constants simultaneously in all ℎh are not required by the irrationality criterion.

The following published results on prime gaps address a different shape of question. Zhang’s bounded-gap theorem [21] produces infinitely many bounded consecutive-prime gaps. Maynard bounds lim inf𝑛(𝑝𝑛+𝑚 −𝑝𝑛)lim infn(pn+m−pn) for every fixed 𝑚m, giving bounded clusters of every fixed size [16], with the explicit unconditional bound lim inf𝑛(𝑝𝑛+1 −𝑝𝑛) ≤600lim infn(pn+1−pn)≤600 . Polymath subsequently improved this to 246246 ; neither numerical bound controls the signed weighted tails required here. The large-gap theorem of Ford, Green, Konyagin, Maynard and Tao gives an effective lower bound for the largest single consecutive-prime gap below 𝑋X [8]. A theorem giving bounded clusters at each fixed cluster size does not by itself supply a weighted condition on windows whose length grows with the basepoint, and none of these results is used as a proof input here.

Conditionally the picture is different. Tao’s comment names uniform quantitative prime-tuples control of about log⁡log⁡𝑛log⁡log⁡n consecutive gaps as the plausible route [23], and Land’s draft carries that out under Kuperberg’s uniform prime-tuples conjecture . The obstructions of Section 8 say which unconditional substitutes cannot replace that hypothesis.

An elementary polynomial bound for the primes

We prove 𝑝𝑛 ≤1250(𝑛 +1)4pn≤1250(n+1)4 for every 𝑛 ≥0n≥0 by the central binomial coefficient method of Erdős’s proof of Chebyshev’s theorem . Let 𝜋(𝑥)π(x) count the primes at most 𝑥x. For an integer 𝑚 ≥4m≥4,

4𝑚<𝑚(2𝑚𝑚)≤𝑚(2𝑚)𝜋(2𝑚).(9)(9)4m<m(2mm)≤m(2m)π(2m).

For the first inequality, 𝑚(2𝑚𝑚)/4𝑚m(2mm)/4m equals 70/6470/64 at 𝑚 =4m=4 and its ratio at successive indices is (2𝑚 +1)/(2𝑚) >1(2m+1)/(2m)>1. For the second, the exponent of a prime ℓℓ in (2𝑚𝑚)(2mm) is ∑𝑘≥1(⌊2𝑚/ℓ𝑘⌋ −2⌊𝑚/ℓ𝑘⌋)∑k≥1(⌊2m/ℓk⌋−2⌊m/ℓk⌋), each summand is 00 or 11, and every summand with ℓ𝑘 >2𝑚ℓk>2m vanishes; hence each prime power dividing (2𝑚𝑚)(2mm) is at most 2𝑚2m, and there are 𝜋(2𝑚)π(2m) of them.

Now fix 𝑛 ≥0n≥0, put 𝑥 =𝑛 +5x=n+5 and 𝑚 =𝑥4 ≥625m=x4≥625, and suppose 𝜋(2𝑚) ≤𝑛π(2m)≤n. Since 𝑥 ≤2𝑥x≤2x and 𝑛 +4(𝑛 +1)𝑥 =4𝑥2 −15𝑥 −5 ≤2𝑥4n+4(n+1)x=4x2−15x−5≤2x4,

𝑚(2𝑚)𝑛=2𝑛𝑥4(𝑛+1)≤2𝑛+4(𝑛+1)𝑥≤22𝑥4=4𝑚,m(2m)n=2nx4(n+1)≤2n+4(n+1)x≤22x4=4m,

Integer certificates

The following calculation uses trial division and integer arithmetic only. It reproduces the two rows of Proposition 6.6 and every inequality used in Theorem 7.1. The four literals are the certificate the Lean kernel decides in KernelDenominatorFloor.lean; their use here requires no floating-point approximation. Adjacent quoted strings are concatenated by Python.

from math import isqrt

primes = [n for n in range(2, 10000)
          if all(n % d for d in range(2, isqrt(n) + 1))]
gaps = [q - p for p, q in zip(primes, primes[1:])]
P = lambda x: x**4 + 8*x**3 + 36*x*x + 104*x + 150
Q = 2**40
expected = [(-662838684750, 11764181250),
            (873345886050, 12805761250)]
for N, target in zip((2, 3), expected):
    D = sum((gaps[N+1+j] - gaps[N+j])*2**(40-j)
            for j in range(1, 41))
    B = 1250*(P(N+43) + P(N+42))
    distance = min(D % Q, Q - D % Q)
    if (D, B) != target or not (abs(D)+B < Q and B < distance):
        raise ArithmeticError("tail certificate failed")
if gaps[4] == gaps[3]:
    raise ArithmeticError("gap mismatch failed")

u = int(
    "8065641857152652932176019632186898003271162829171466334827"
    "3083607794415278717445033509407855988903369988525550746159"
    "7355889792250084202344821020139160956663658789718168152662"
    "0217"
)

v = int(
    "2194945124413663232143970924541263312422069524635615360518"
    "4247077351958221816830720189289904831662955084392690248683"
    "1216291723988537733235173040607254496838530213867781442335"
    "1745"
)

up = int(
    "6539437101498162626882411892470905222108260008568555445975"
    "3026163315521784668689909712759876562484620059098138417469"
    "5232839888185316374272333277389611483117334000493867584923"
    "912"
)

vp = int(
    "1779611075789866551198427241621709630120136323281598176637"
    "8490605249229735501968764904036152970729491656650873938580"
    "6203025466313389810291243786005499164537499383612081805160"
    "767"
)

c = len(primes)
A = sum(p*2**(c-1-i) for i, p in enumerate(primes))
checks = (c == 1229,
          u > 0 and v > 0 and up > 0 and vp > 0,
          up*v - u*vp == 1,
          u*2**c < A*v,
          (2*A + 5000*(c+1)**4)*vp < up*2**(c+1),
          v+vp >= 2**589,
          2**589 > 10**177)
if not all(checks):
    raise ArithmeticError("denominator certificate failed")
print("Both tail rows and the denominator floor verified.")

Each link identifies its own immutable source revision. Named declaration links have been refreshed from the supplied checked index; historical computation links retain their separate receipt pins. Extended record: displaced results, ordinary proofs and corrections

The totient witness and forward propagation

The note states the exact denominator law (6) and uses it directly. The classical witness that produced it is worth recording, because it is the form in which the shift length first appears.

Proposition D.1 (a shift of totient length). Let 𝑇 :ℕ →ℚT:N→Q satisfy the dyadic tail recurrence with integer digits. If the reduced denominator 𝑑d of 𝑇𝑁TN is odd, then 𝜎𝜑(𝑑)(𝑁)σφ(d)(N) is an integer.

Proof. Since 𝑑d is odd, 22 and 𝑑d are coprime, so Euler’s congruence gives 𝑑 ∣2𝜑(𝑑) −1d∣2φ(d)−1. Writing 2𝜑(𝑑) −1 =𝑑𝑘2φ(d)−1=dk and 𝑇𝑁 =𝑢/𝑑TN=u/d in lowest terms, (2𝜑(𝑑) −1)𝑇𝑁 =𝑘𝑢(2φ(d)−1)TN=ku is an integer, and the integral-shift criterion transfers this to the shift. ◻

Proposition D.2 (propagation). Let 𝑇 :ℕ →ℝT:N→R satisfy 𝑇𝑛+1 =2𝑇𝑛 −𝑎𝑛+1Tn+1=2Tn−an+1 with integer digits, and define 𝜎ℎ(𝑁) =𝑇𝑁+ℎ −𝑇𝑁σh(N)=TN+h−TN. For fixed ℎ,𝑁 ≥0h,N≥0, if 𝜎ℎ(𝑁)σh(N) is an integer, then 𝜎ℎ(𝑁 +𝑘)σh(N+k) is an integer for every 𝑘 ≥0k≥0.

Proof. The shift step identity gives 𝜎ℎ(𝑁 +1) =2𝜎ℎ(𝑁) −(𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1 −𝑔𝑁+1)σh(N+1)=2σh(N)−(gN+h+1−gN+1), an integer combination of an integer and two digits. Induct on 𝑘k. ◻

These are the totient shift and the propagation theorems cited in the note. Two worked instances. If den⁡𝑇𝑁 =3den⁡TN=3 then 𝜑(3) =2φ(3)=2 and 3𝑇𝑁3TN is an integer, so 𝜎2(𝑁)σ2(N) is integral while 𝜎1(𝑁)σ1(N) is not; if den⁡𝑇𝑁 =5den⁡TN=5 then 𝜎4(𝑁)σ4(N) is integral. In the orbit with every digit zero and 𝑇0 =1/12T0=1/12, the denominator is 12 =22 ⋅312=22⋅3, the orbit reaches 𝑇2 =1/3T2=1/3 with odd denominator at 𝑠 =2s=2, and ℎ =𝜑(3) =2h=φ(3)=2 is exactly the shift length seen to be integral from index 22 onwards. The totient is a witness rather than the classification: the exact criterion is den⁡(𝑇𝑁) ∣2ℎ −1den⁡(TN)∣2h−1, and the least admissible ℎh is the multiplicative order of 22 modulo the odd part.

one has

where 𝐷ℎ,𝑁,𝐿mod2𝐿Dh,N,Lmod2L is the least nonnegative residue, including when 𝐷ℎ,𝑁,𝐿 <0Dh,N,L<0. The finite criterion therefore asks the residue of 𝐷ℎ,𝑁,𝐿Dh,N,L to avoid the two arcs of radius 2𝐿𝑅ℎ,𝑁,𝐿(𝑀)2LRh,N,L(M) around 00 modulo 2𝐿2L. A one-block certificate would be a prime-gap theorem producing such an avoided arc on a logarithmic block. This rewriting is paper-level and carries no Lean declaration.

Proposition D.4 (completeness of finite separation). Suppose 𝐷 ∈ℝD∈R, 𝑆𝐿 ∈ℝSL∈R and 𝑅𝐿 ≥0RL≥0 satisfy |𝐷 −𝑆𝐿| ≤𝑅𝐿|D−SL|≤RL and 𝑅𝐿 →0RL→0. Then

𝐷∉ℤ⟺there exists 𝐿 with dist⁡(𝑆𝐿,ℤ)>𝑅𝐿.D∉Z⟺there exists L with dist⁡(SL,Z)>RL.

Proof. The reverse implication follows from the triangle inequality. For the forward implication put 𝛿 =dist⁡(𝐷,ℤ) >0δ=dist⁡(D,Z)>0 and choose 𝑅𝐿 <𝛿/2RL<δ/2. The distance to ℤZ is 11-Lipschitz, so dist⁡(𝑆𝐿,ℤ) ≥𝛿 −𝑅𝐿 >𝑅𝐿dist⁡(SL,Z)≥δ−RL>RL. ◻

Thus existence of an arbitrarily deep finite certificate is an exact reformulation of nonintegrality, not a new prime-gap estimate. A useful analytic producer must control the separation as well as the tail.

Divisor-hitting shift escape

Problem D.5 (divisor-hitting shift escape). For every 𝑟 ≥1r≥1, does some positive multiple of 𝑟r escape cofinally, in the sense of (7) at shift length 𝑚𝑟mr for some 𝑚 ≥1m≥1?

This is an exact reformulation, not a weaker mathematical target. If 𝑇0T0 is irrational, every positive shift is nonintegral by the block identity, so divisor-hitting escape follows with 𝑚 =1m=1. Conversely, rationality gives a shift ℎ ≥1h≥1 that is integral at every sufficiently late index. For each positive integer 𝑚m, the identity

𝑇𝑁+𝑚ℎ−𝑇𝑁=𝑚−1∑𝑗=0(𝑇𝑁+(𝑗+1)ℎ−𝑇𝑁+𝑗ℎ)TN+mh−TN=∑j=0m−1(TN+(j+1)h−TN+jh)

makes every multiple 𝑚ℎmh eventually integral. Taking 𝑟 =ℎr=h contradicts divisor-hitting escape. This ordinary deduction uses the checked rationality classification and a finite telescope; rearranging the quantifiers supplies no new estimate for the actual prime gaps.

Two ordinary proofs about the free-pair producer

Both arguments below are ordinary mathematical deductions. The first uses the prime number theorem, while the second consumes the free-pair lattice proved above. Neither deduction is claimed to be kernel-checked; the exact tail recurrence and free-pair statements they use have their separate linked Lean evidence.

State compression.

Exchanging the order of summation gives ∑𝑁≤𝑋𝑇𝑁 ≤(𝑝𝑋+1 −𝑝0) +2𝑇𝑋∑N≤XTN≤(pX+1−p0)+2TX. The prime number theorem [17] also gives

𝑇𝑋𝑝𝑋=∑𝑗≥1𝑔𝑋+𝑗2𝑗𝑝𝑋⟶0.(10)(10)TXpX=∑j≥1gX+j2jpX⟶0.

Indeed, for each fixed 𝑗j the summand without 2−𝑗2−j tends to zero because 𝑝𝑋+𝑗/𝑝𝑋 →1pX+j/pX→1. The usual two-sided bounds 𝑝𝑛 ≍𝑛log⁡𝑛pn≍nlog⁡n dominate 𝑔𝑋+𝑗/𝑝𝑋gX+j/pX by 𝐾(1 +𝑗)2K(1+j)2, independently of 𝑋X; multiplication by 2−𝑗2−j therefore permits dominated convergence. Applying the first-moment bound at 2𝑋2X and using long251:eq:tail-small-relative-prime, there is an absolute 𝐾0K0 such that

∑𝑋<𝑁≤2𝑋𝑇𝑁≤𝐾0𝑋log⁡𝑋∑X<N≤2XTN≤K0Xlog⁡X

for all large 𝑋X. Thus, for each fixed 𝐶 >1C>1, Markov’s inequality leaves at least (1 −1/𝐶)𝑋(1−1/C)X indices in (𝑋,2𝑋](X,2X] with 𝑇𝑁 ≤𝐾0𝐶log⁡𝑋TN≤K0Clog⁡X.

Under rationality, take 𝑋X beyond the point where the reduced denominator is the fixed odd integer 𝑑d. On this set 𝑇𝑁TN lies in 𝑑−1ℤ≥0d−1Z≥0 and takes at most 𝑑𝐾0𝐶log⁡𝑋 +1dK0Clog⁡X+1 values. Pigeonhole therefore gives one value at ≫𝐶,𝑑𝑋/log⁡𝑋≫C,dX/log⁡X indices. This compression uses the growth of the actual primes. It is false for a general rational integer-digit orbit: the quadratic countermodel of Proposition 8.9 has the strictly increasing tails 𝑇𝑁 =2(𝑁 +4)2TN=2(N+4)2. Even for the primes, equal-tail pairs have difference zero and hence do not supply the nonintegral difference required by the free-pair criterion. The naive form ∑𝑁≤𝑋𝑇𝑁 ≤𝑝𝑋+1∑N≤XTN≤pX+1 is false.

Redundancy of the gap condition.

Under the free-pair lattice the difference 𝑇𝑀 −𝑇𝑁TM−TN is an integer whenever the modulus divides the offset, and an integer cannot lie in (12,1)(12,1). The half-window component of the reduced event of Theorem 6.4 is therefore already a contradiction on its own, and the gap-mismatch condition adds nothing to it. That changes which component a proof has to produce.

A bounded companion to the recurring-values countermodel

Theorem 8.8 carries a logarithmic growth profile so that its cumulative sequence matches the primes. The mechanism is visible in a much smaller example, which is recorded here because it is checkable by hand.

Proposition D.6 (bounded recurring-values countermodel). Put 𝑈0 =4U0=4 and, for 𝑛 ≥1n≥1, 𝑈𝑛 =6Un=6 when 𝑛 =𝑘!n=k! for some 𝑘 ≥3k≥3 and 𝑈𝑛 =4Un=4 otherwise, and set 𝑎𝑛 =2𝑈𝑛−1 −𝑈𝑛an=2Un−1−Un for 𝑛 ≥1n≥1. Then 𝑎𝑛 ∈{2,4,8}an∈{2,4,8}, the value 22 occurs at every index 𝑘!k! and the value 44 at every index 2 𝑘!2k!, so both recur infinitely often at indices divisible by any fixed 𝑡 ≥1t≥1. The series ∑𝑛≥1𝑎𝑛2−𝑛∑n≥1an2−n equals 44 and every tail ∑𝑗≥1𝑎𝑁+𝑗2−𝑗∑j≥1aN+j2−j equals the integer 𝑈𝑁UN.

Proof. For 𝑘 ≥3k≥3 the index 𝑘!k! is even and at least 66, and 𝑘! −1k!−1 is odd, so the predecessor of a spike is an ordinary index; hence 𝑎𝑘! =8 −6 =2ak!=8−6=2, 𝑎𝑘!+1 =12 −4 =8ak!+1=12−4=8, and 𝑎𝑛 =8 −4 =4an=8−4=4 elsewhere. For 𝑘 ≥2k≥2 one has 𝑘! <2 𝑘! <(𝑘 +1)!k!<2k!<(k+1)!, so 2 𝑘!2k! is not a factorial, and 2 𝑘! −12k!−1 is odd so it is not a factorial either; therefore 𝑎2𝑘! =4a2k!=4. Since 𝑡 ∣𝑘!t∣k! for every large 𝑘k, both values recur in the residue class 00 modulo 𝑡t. The identity 𝑎𝑛2−𝑛 =𝑈𝑛−12−(𝑛−1) −𝑈𝑛2−𝑛an2−n=Un−12−(n−1)−Un2−n telescopes to ∑𝑚𝑗=1𝑎𝑁+𝑗2−𝑗 =𝑈𝑁 −𝑈𝑁+𝑚2−𝑚∑j=1maN+j2−j=UN−UN+m2−m, and 𝑈U is bounded, so the endpoint vanishes. ◻

The cumulative sequence of this word grows linearly, which is the one property that separates it from the primes and the reason the note carries the logarithmic version instead. Both refute the same generic implication.

Corrections to earlier records

Two different improvements to the exclusion record.

An earlier internal record gave a denominator exclusion at 1060210602. The kernel-decided floor 2589 >101772589>10177 of Theorem 7.1 is numerically smaller but has a different verification status. It does not supersede 1060210602 in numerical strength. The continued-fraction exclusion 239997 >1012040239997>1012040 of Theorem 7.2 is the larger numerical bound. Its receipt’s digit count 1204112041 must not be substituted for the exponent 1204012040. The independent integer replay supplied with this revision reproduces the stated larger exclusion by a separate interval and Farey-neighbour calculation; it is not a new Lean replay.

The named missing input.

An earlier record named Hardy-Littlewood 𝑘k-tuple correlation of consecutive gaps at a fixed offset as the missing input. With the offset freed by Theorem 5.5 the route needs, for each modulus 𝑡t, cofinally many congruent pairs with certified nonintegral tail difference. A further record proposed that two even values differing by 22, each occurring infinitely often inside a common index residue class, would supply the two-condition form. No proof of that implication was ever produced, and Theorem 8.8 shows that no proof exists at the level of integer-digit recurrences. That entry is withdrawn.

The formal boundary.

An earlier reading of the short note placed the real-tail bridge and the real form of the adjacent-pair consumer on the paper side. Both are kernel-checked, at line 48 and line 99 of the real prime-gap tail module. A second reading placed the kernel-decided denominator floor and the free-pair criterion outside the source revision the note pins. Both modules are present at that revision, and both are linked from the note.

Complete affine-lattice statement from the short note

The following expands the compact circularity statement formerly printed in the body of this record. In particular the fixed-lattice predicate and its strict growth hypothesis are stated, not left implicit.

Here 𝐷𝑁 =𝜎ℎ(𝑁)DN=σh(N) and 𝛿𝑁 =𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1 −𝑔𝑁+1δN=gN+h+1−gN+1, with ℎh fixed. For a longer block, set

𝐵ℎ,𝑁,𝑟=𝑟−1∑𝑖=02𝑟−1−𝑖𝛿𝑁+𝑖;𝐷𝑁+𝑟=2𝑟𝐷𝑁−𝐵ℎ,𝑁,𝑟.Bh,N,r=∑i=0r−12r−1−iδN+i;DN+r=2rDN−Bh,N,r.

Call the data-dependent affine condition

A𝑁,𝑟:𝐷𝑁+𝑟∈−𝐵ℎ,𝑁,𝑟+2𝑟+1ℤ.AN,r:DN+r∈−Bh,N,r+2r+1Z.

Theorem E.1 (affine and fixed-lattice circularity). For every rational dyadic tail recurrence and all ℎ,𝑁,𝑟 ≥0h,N,r≥0,

A𝑁,𝑟⟺𝐷𝑁∈2ℤ.(11)(11)AN,r⟺DN∈2Z.

Consequently, if every 𝛿𝑁δN is even, then

(∀𝑁0 ∃𝑁,𝑟: 𝑁0<𝑁 and ¬A𝑁,𝑟)⟺𝐷𝑁∉ℤ for arbitrarily large 𝑁.(12)(12)(∀N0 ∃N,r: N0<N and ¬AN,r)⟺DN∉Z for arbitrarily large N.

There is a second equivalence. Let 𝑏 :ℕ →ℚb:N→Q satisfy |𝐷𝑁| ≤𝑏(𝑁)|DN|≤b(N) for every 𝑁N, and suppose that for every 𝑁N and every positive integer 𝑞q there is an 𝑟r with

2𝑏(𝑁+𝑟)𝑞<2𝑟.(13)(13)2b(N+r)q<2r.

Then

∀𝑁0 ∃𝑁,𝑟: 𝑁0<𝑁 and ∀𝑧∈ℤ,𝑏(𝑁+𝑟)<|𝐵ℎ,𝑁,𝑟−2𝑟𝑧|⟺𝐷𝑁∉ℤ for arbitrarily large 𝑁.(14)(14)∀N0 ∃N,r: N0<N and ∀z∈Z,b(N+r)<|Bh,N,r−2rz|⟺DN∉Z for arbitrarily large N.

Proof. Substituting 𝐷𝑁+𝑟 =2𝑟𝐷𝑁 −𝐵ℎ,𝑁,𝑟DN+r=2rDN−Bh,N,r into A𝑁,𝑟AN,r cancels the observed block from both sides and leaves 𝐷𝑁 =2𝑧DN=2z. This proves (11). After one recurrence step, evenness of 𝛿𝑁δN identifies even integrality at 𝑁 +1N+1 with ordinary integrality at 𝑁N. The forward implication in (12) follows, while the reverse implication chooses a nonintegral 𝐷𝑁DN and the legal depth 𝑟 =0r=0.

For (14), eventual integrality and the block identity give some 𝑧 ∈ℤz∈Z with

𝐵ℎ,𝑁,𝑟−2𝑟𝑧=−𝐷𝑁+𝑟,Bh,N,r−2rz=−DN+r,

so the displayed strict separation contradicts |𝐷𝑁+𝑟| ≤𝑏(𝑁 +𝑟)|DN+r|≤b(N+r). Conversely, if 𝐷𝑁DN is nonintegral and has reduced denominator 𝑞q, then its distance from every integer is at least 1/𝑞1/q. Choose 𝑟r from (13), scale this separation by 2𝑟2r, and use the block identity together with |𝐷𝑁+𝑟| ≤𝑏(𝑁 +𝑟)|DN+r|≤b(N+r). The triangle inequality gives |𝐵ℎ,𝑁,𝑟 −2𝑟𝑧| >𝑏(𝑁 +𝑟)|Bh,N,r−2rz|>b(N+r) for every integer 𝑧z. ◻

The three displayed equivalences are assembled in one declaration, affine circularity bundle.

The first equivalence shows that the apparent affine hierarchy contains no depth-dependent information: it is the pullback of even integrality through the recurrence identity. The fixed lattice removes that data dependence, but under the stated growth condition rational denominator separation already forces every required escape. Hence neither cofinal condition is an independent source of information about consecutive primes.

Mathematical and evidence map

Perturbations.

The bounded construction and the sparse congruence-preserving theorem are existence results for altered integer words. Their conclusion is not a prime-producing construction. The ordinary sparse proof and the formal existence proof have different witnesses.

Exact criteria.

Summation by parts identifies the actual tails. Integral-shift, free-pair and lcm-diagonal criteria then classify rationality at the recurrence level. Their equivalence does not supply the missing prime-specific witnesses.

Obstructions.

Polynomial growth, bounded residues, fixed-block nonconcentration and recurring gap values do not by themselves force the needed tail behaviour. The numbered constructions above give the precise counterexamples.

Certificates.

Finite window comparisons and denominator exclusions are exact finite statements once the proved analytic remainder bounds are supplied. A large rational-denominator floor is not an irrationality theorem.

Formal evidence.

The revision’s declaration ledger records the file, line, immutable revision and supplied build status of each linked declaration. The older administrative family catalogue is retained verbatim with that ledger; counts of registry rows or project-wide families do not strengthen any mathematical statement.
